newsitem.title: USA: NCAA BASKETBALL-TATTOOS AND EARRINGS TOPIC FOR MINNESOTA'S HASKINS.
newsitem.headline: NCAA BASKETBALL-TATTOOS AND EARRINGS TOPIC FOR MINNESOTA'S HASKINS.

text.p: Dennis Rodman, are you listening?

Minnesota coach Clem Haskins was asked more about earrings and tattoos Friday than about the Kentucky pressing defence he was to face the next night in the second game of the NCAA basketball semifinals.

"I'm a strong believer in no tattoos," said Haskins. "Yes, I have kids with tattoos, yes, I have some kids that wear earrings, but they wear them in their private surroundings. They know there's a time and place for everything."
He admitted that his star Bobby Jackson has tattoos. "He's got tattoos all over his body but they were there in high school.
"I think the trend in America is kind of sick because we don't have strong enough people to stand up for what's right and what's wrong. And we need more of that in our school system."

"Well it's great to be a player under a great coach like Coach Haskins," said Jackson. "He brings so much to the game. And everybody knows his style and we respect that. And if we didn't respect that we wouldn't be here."
He noted that he had his tattoo before he arrived in college while teammate Courtney James got one after.
"Coach don't like tattoos and earrings. But we understand that. But no way we can take them off, so we're going to have to stick with it."
Kentucky players were asked if they thought earrings and tattoos meant players were undisciplined.
"I don't think so, not really," said Jared Prickett. "I think there's quite a few guys on the team that have tattoos on our team. I'm not one, but there's a few guys.
"And I think they have the same discipline as anyone else on the team. That's freedom of speech, I guess."

Kentucky's NBA-bound superstar Ron Mercer said of Haskins' remarks: "The times have changed since he's been in college. I wouldn't say a person is less disciplined by certain things they do or what they have on their bodies. It's their choice."
Haskins said it was a matter of respect for basketball.
"This game has meant everything to me. I never wanted to be a president, lawyer or doctor. I wanted to play basketball and be a coach and work with young people.

"I think today we've let coaches be disrespectful of the game if they let people do things. Everybody is a copycat. And the coaches are copycat, they'll sell out for anything. I don't think that's right. And I will never do that."
Haskins said he is looking for a certain kind of player at Minnesota.

"If you look at our programme, we have quality players. And I think young players are looking for direction, they want to be disciplined. I think there's a right way and wrong way to do everything. We have a lot of fun at Minnesota."
He mentioned that his attitudes had not prevented him from attracting Courtney James, who is from Indianapolis.
"It was a bigtime recruit for us and that's why I say we have quality players," said Haskins.

"He's from a one-parent home and I think his mother was looking for discipline. He needed a man figure in his life and a strong individual lilke Clem Haskins to deal with him so he could grow as a young man.

"There's more to life to me than a jump shot and rebounding and winning a national championship. When I retire don't measure me by how much championships I win but assess me by the young people that played for me.
But pressed again about what is wrong with earrings, he replied: "I think earrings were made for ladies to wear, not for men. And I won't change from that."
He presented a scenario where he might lose his job by refusing to bend his rules when a great, earring-deprived player came along -- Michael Jordan comes to mind -- but said he would remain adamant.
And as for that other Chicago Bull, Dennis Rodman, of the tattoos, earrings, bridal dresses....

"I think if you look at all the problems he's having, I think it speaks for itself," Haskins said of Rodman. "I don't think we need role models like that in this country. Not a very good example, I don't think.
"He's a great player, I admire his play, I love him as a player, but his stand on things makes me think I would not enjoy being around him."
